I would keep my farm centered on the standard Quzhou pattern: winter wheat followed by summer maize. In my place, that is still the most dependable way to use land, irrigation, machinery, and labor efficiently across the full year. I would not spread myself across too many specialty crops, because at 55 I would prefer a system that is proven, mechanizable, and easier to manage well. Since I have a university education, I would run it in a more disciplined way: improved or hybrid seed, moderate but sufficient fertilizer, irrigation timed to key growth stages instead of excessive watering, and pesticide use only as needed to keep risk under control. I will assume I am managing 100 mu. I would put all 100 mu into winter wheat first, then follow with summer maize on the same 100 mu after wheat harvest. For wheat, I would aim for stable yield with plough tillage, solid base fertilizer, and about three irrigations at overwintering recovery, jointing, and grain filling if moisture requires it. For maize, I would switch to hybrid seed, use a little more potassium support, keep irrigation lower than wheat unless drought forces extra watering, and control weeds and insects with a few targeted applications. My goal is not the highest possible yield on paper; it is steady output, manageable costs, and low production risk.
